Designing the Application Structure
Rather than creating dozens of folders upfront, I started with only the folders that were truly required.
src/app
│
├── core
├── shared
├── layout
├── features
└── modelsEach folder has a clear responsibility.
Core
Contains application-wide infrastructure that exists only once.
Examples:

• Authentication Guards

• HTTP Interceptors

• Global Error Handling

• Application Configuration
Shared
Contains reusable UI elements that can be shared across multiple features.
Examples:

• Buttons

• Loaders

• Dialogs

• Toast Messages
Layout
Contains the application’s common shell such as:

• Header

• Sidebar

• Footer
One important realization was:
Login is not part of the layout.
Login belongs to the Authentication feature because it represents business functionality, while the layout represents the application’s common structure.
Features
Business modules live inside the Features folder.
Instead of creating every future module upfront, I created only what was needed today.
features
└── authenticationThis follows the idea of letting the architecture evolve naturally rather than creating many empty folders.

Creating the First Feature
Using Angular CLI, I generated the Login component inside the Authentication feature.
ng generate component features/authentication/loginDuring this step, I encountered an unexpected issue.
File ng.ps1 cannot be loaded because running scripts is disabled on this system.Since VS Code was using PowerShell, I used the following workaround:
ng.cmd generate component features/authentication/loginThis worked successfully, and later I plan to configure PowerShell execution policies properly.
